39: Event catering in the United States runs on two engines that peak at different times. Companies book during the work week: drop-off lunches, buffets, receptions and year-end parties. Private clients book on weekends: weddings, rehearsal dinners, birthdays and celebrations of life. Search data points the same way, since buyers look up wedding, corporate and event catering thousands of times every month. This plan describes a full-service caterer that serves both groups without running a restaurant. We cook in a permitted shared commissary kitchen, deliver in a refrigerated van and serve at the client's venue, so what we sell is a well-run event, not a dining room.
40: The concept is a full-service, off-site event caterer. We rent a shared commissary kitchen by the hour, load a used refrigerated cargo van and serve wherever the client holds the event. Five service styles cover the range: drop-off, buffet, family-style, plated and chef-attended stations. The stations are what set us apart. A taco bar, a carving station, a pasta station or a poke bar with a cook working in front of the guests supports a higher price per guest than a plain buffet, and it gives clients something to photograph and talk about. We do not hold an alcohol license: the client buys the alcohol and certified bartenders serve it, backed by liquor liability insurance.
41: The total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} in startup costs plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The biggest lines are the refrigerated van and its cooling unit, our own kitchen equipment, chafing dishes and insulated carriers, and the first-year permits. We do not build or lease a kitchen of our own, which keeps the investment far below the $250,000 or more that restroworks.com associates with a caterer that owns its kitchen, vehicles and staff. The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. We cover it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years.
42: In year 1 we plan {{eventos_a1}} events with an average of {{invitados_evento}} guests at {{precio_invitado}} per guest, excluding sales tax. That adds up to {{ventas_a1}} in revenue, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, and the lowest debt service coverage over the loan term is {{dscr_min}}. On an accounting basis the business breaks even at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. Wedding dates are booked months ahead and companies reorder, which gives the calendar more visibility than a walk-up business has.
43: The founding team is an owner who works as executive chef and also sells, a sous chef who runs the kitchen, a pool of hourly event staff on the payroll, and a prep cook who doubles as the van driver. That makes {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. Event staff are W-2 employees scheduled event by event, so labor cost rises and falls with the number of events. Replace this paragraph with your own background: a lender wants to see who has run a kitchen and who has sold events. The plan shows that a caterer without a restaurant can start with controlled risk, as long as every event is quoted, deposited and staffed on purpose.
46: Our clients buy an event that goes well, not just food. The first group is companies: office managers, HR teams and event planners who need a lunch, a reception or a year-end party handled without surprises. The second group is private clients planning a wedding, a rehearsal dinner, a milestone birthday or a celebration of life, who want one point of contact for the menu, the staff and the timeline. Both groups care about the same things: safe food that arrives on time, staff who look after the guests, and a quote with no surprises. The difference is the sales cycle. Companies reorder, while couples book once, months ahead.
47: Our value proposition rests on three pillars. First, chef-attended themed stations. A taco bar, a carving station, pasta finished to order or a poke bar turns the meal into part of the entertainment, and a cook in front of the guests can explain each dish and answer allergy questions on the spot. Second, special diets handled as part of the menu, not as an exception. Vegan, gluten-free and halal dishes are planned and plated with the same care as the main menu, and allergens are written into every quote. Third, a tasting before the contract and a menu that reflects the client, from a company's colors and theme to a couple's family recipes. Each pillar gives us a reason to charge for the experience, not only for the food.
48: We quote the price per guest excluding sales tax and with service included, and the average is {{precio_invitado}}. With {{invitados_evento}} guests per event, the average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. We keep the service charge, which is part of our price and pays for the crew, separate from voluntary gratuity, which belongs to the staff and stays out of our margin. A deposit blocks the date. We set it at 35% in this kit as an estimate, while sample catering contracts commonly ask for 25-50% at signing. No deposit, no date on the calendar.
49: We compete against three alternatives. Restaurants that cater on the side are convenient, but their kitchen and staff serve the dining room first, and they rarely offer stations or full service at a venue. Large caterers bring scale and venue relationships, though they often work with set menus and high minimums. Corporate catering marketplaces make ordering easy for companies and take a commission on every order. We position ourselves in the gap: a small team with a chef at the station, flexible menus and one person responsible for the event from the quote to the pack-down. Mobile food vendors sell a different product, so we do not compete with them on speed or price per plate.
50: We offer five service styles so the client can match the event to the budget. Drop-off is the lightest: we deliver the food ready to eat. A buffet adds setup and attendants. Family-style puts shared platters on every table, plated adds servers and tighter timing, and chef-attended stations add a cook in front of the guests. Each style has a guest minimum, because small orders do not cover the kitchen hours and the van. The pricing calculator in this kit builds the quote for each style from your own costs, so the price per guest is never a guess.
53: Demand for catering in the United States comes from two sides, and search data shows both. Each month, people in the U.S. search for wedding catering about 22,200 times, corporate catering about 6,600 times, event catering about 3,600 times and drop-off catering about 1,300 times (DataForSEO, October 2026). These are searches by buyers, not by people who want to start a business, so they confirm the two engines of this plan: private celebrations and company orders. We do not quote a total market size, because the figures change with every source and definition. What matters for a small caterer is local: how many weddings, offices and venues sit within an hour of your commissary kitchen.
54: Private clients are the more emotional buyers. According to The Knot 2025 Real Weddings Study, reported by Fox Business, couples spent an average of $80 per plate on wedding catering in 2024. Around the wedding come rehearsal dinners, engagement parties and showers, and beyond it milestone birthdays, anniversaries and celebrations of life. These clients compare menus, ask for a tasting and read reviews before they sign, so the sales cycle is long and the first conversation matters. Weddings cluster in the warmer months and in early fall, which is why the seasonal curve in the workbook is uneven and why we plan cash around it.
55: Corporate clients buy on a different logic. They order drop-off and boxed lunches for meetings, buffets for training days, receptions for openings and parties at the end of the year. The buyer is usually an office manager, an HR lead or an event planner who needs a reliable vendor and an invoice that fits company rules. Companies often pay on 30-day terms, so the workbook assumes {{cobro_dias}} days of average collection and the cash-flow sheet shows what that costs in working capital. Many companies also order through corporate catering marketplaces, and the example gives them {{marketplace_pct}} of sales at a {{marketplace_comision}} commission.
56: In the example case, companies account for about three of every four events and about half of the sales. This is a kit estimate, not market data: private events are fewer but larger, so each one carries more revenue. The calendar is uneven too. The example opens in March, so Month 1 is March, and the curve peaks in October and December, with the weakest months in January and February and a slower stretch in midsummer. Your local calendar will differ, so rotate the curve to your opening month and replace the shares with what your own bookings suggest.
57: A few trends are worth watching, without leaning on numbers we cannot source. Clients ask more often for vegan, gluten-free and allergy-safe menus, and they expect the caterer to handle them without drama. Live experiences such as carving and pasta stations give a reception something to look at. Compostable disposables and less waste are becoming part of the conversation for companies and couples alike. We treat these as reasons to design the menu well, not as claims about growth.
58: Demand carries risks that the plan should name. Wedding season is short, so a slow spring can leave a gap that fall cannot fully fill. Clients cancel or shrink the guest count late, which is why the deposit and the cancellation terms matter. Corporate budgets can freeze in a weak quarter, and a single large account can distort a year. We reduce these risks by mixing private and company clients, by collecting deposits and by keeping fixed costs light.
61: Before you price anything, map who competes within an hour of your commissary kitchen. The list usually includes established caterers with a wedding reputation, restaurants that cater on the side, corporate catering marketplaces that put many vendors in front of the same buyer, and grocery-store party trays for the lowest budgets. Each one answers a different need, and writing them down tells you where a small, chef-led caterer has room.
62: The five forces look like this for an event caterer. Supplier power is low, because food distributors and equipment sellers are plentiful and easy to switch. Buyer power is moderate: clients compare quotes and reviews, and marketplaces make comparison one click away, but a good tasting and a clear proposal build loyalty. The threat of substitutes is real, since a restaurant, a grocery tray or a do-it-yourself party can replace a caterer on a small budget. Rivalry is strongest in wedding season, when local caterers compete for the same dates. The threat of new entrants is moderate. According to restroworks.com, a caterer that rents a shared kitchen starts for a fraction of the $250,000 or more that a caterer with its own kitchen, vehicles and staff needs, but a permitted kitchen, insurance and a refrigerated van still take planning and cash, which keeps casual entrants out.
63: Direct competitors are other full-service caterers that serve the same guest counts and the same venues, along with restaurants that offer catering and large regional caterers. Indirect competitors are grocery party trays, meal-delivery apps and clients who cook for themselves. To compare yourself fairly, line up price per guest, what the price includes, the service style, the minimum guest count and the reviews on The Knot, WeddingWire and Google. Then decide where you win: the chef-attended station, the tasting, the response time or the clarity of the quote. Say it in one sentence and use it everywhere.
64: The barriers to entry are mostly about compliance and cash. A caterer needs a permitted commercial kitchen and a written agreement to use it, because catering from a home kitchen is not allowed. For example, one California county health department requires catering operations to use a permitted kitchen and prohibits preparing the food at home. Insurance is the second barrier: general liability or a business owner's policy, commercial auto, workers' compensation and, when alcohol is served, liquor liability. Events often need their own permits, and a trained crew takes time to build. These barriers protect caterers who have already done the work.
65: Four factors decide whether a caterer succeeds. The first is reliability: arriving on time, with the right quantities and the setup the client approved. The second is food safety in transport, because hot food has to stay hot and cold food cold from the commissary to the venue. The third is reputation, built on reviews after every event. The fourth is relationships with venues and wedding planners, who steer many bookings and remember who made their day easier. A small caterer that handles these four well can win work from larger competitors.
66: The SWOT analysis for this concept is straightforward. Strengths: low fixed costs, since we rent commissary hours instead of a building, plus a clear differentiator in the chef-attended stations and a mix of company and private clients. Weaknesses: dependence on a few key people, a limited production capacity on the busiest weekends and a calendar that is uneven across the year. Opportunities: corporate clients who want repeat vendors, planners and venues that keep preferred-vendor lists, and clients who value special-diet menus handled well. Threats: a food-safety incident, late cancellations, rising food and labor costs, and marketplaces that push prices down.
69: Our marketing strategy follows two funnels. Weddings and private parties have a long cycle: the client finds us online, asks for a quote, attends a tasting and signs months before the date. Companies have a shorter, repeat-driven cycle: one successful lunch or reception leads to the next order and to a recommendation inside the same office. We treat each funnel differently in message and in channel, but both rest on the same promise: an event that goes smoothly, with a chef you can see at the station.
70: The website is our main sales tool, because clients check it before they call. It shows sample menus for each service style, prices expressed as "from" prices per guest, photos of real events and a short quote form that asks for the date, the venue, the guest count and any dietary needs. Beside it, a complete Google Business Profile with photos, service areas and recent reviews puts us in front of people who search for a caterer nearby. We answer every review, positive or negative, within a day. Consistent photos and clear menus do more than any slogan, and they are cheap to maintain.
71: Directories bring in qualified leads when a profile is complete. For weddings, The Knot and WeddingWire are the places where couples compare caterers, read reviews and send quote requests, so a full profile with photos and menus is worth the effort. For companies, ezCater and similar corporate catering marketplaces put us in front of office managers who order every week, at the cost of a commission, which the workbook models at {{marketplace_comision}} on the share of sales that comes through them. We use marketplaces to find first-time clients and then invite the best ones to order directly.
72: Direct sales to companies work well for a caterer who is willing to knock on doors. Start with office managers, HR teams and event planners within delivery range, and bring a sample lunch with a one-page menu. Visit venues, hotels and wedding planners and ask to be added to their preferred-vendor lists, since a venue that recommends you sends bookings without any advertising cost. Follow every visit with an email and a calendar reminder. A steady rhythm of small contacts each week usually beats one big campaign.
73: Tastings are our closest step to the sale, so we budget for them as a line in the profit and loss statement. We offer them to serious prospects, mainly couples and larger corporate events, with a small portion of each dish and a printed proposal. The proposal sets out the menu, the service style, the staff, the price per guest, the service charge, the deposit and the cancellation terms. After the tasting we follow up within a day, and once the client accepts we send the contract and collect the deposit to hold the date.
74: The best marketing happens after the event. We ask for a review within a few days, while the client still remembers the evening, and we send a short thank-you with a photo when the client agrees. Corporate clients who order regularly get a simple reorder process, with their usual menu saved and a named contact. We ask happy clients for introductions to a friend who is planning a party or a colleague who books events, and we thank them with a small gesture. Repeat clients and referrals cost less to win than any new lead.
75: The example budgets {{marketing_anual}} a year for marketing, mainly for directory listings, photography and a modest amount of search advertising. We track every lead back to its source (website, The Knot, WeddingWire, ezCater, referral or venue) and calculate the marketing cost per event won. If a channel books events at a lower cost, it gets more of the budget, and if it does not, we stop. Review the numbers each quarter and adjust.
